title: U.S.-India Insight: India’s Trade Deals: Only a Starting Point to Progress

We now have several years of trade data to assess the impact of India’s earliest agreements. Clearly, trade agreements alone are not a panacea. While trade with Australia and the United Emirates grew in the years following the deals, their weight in India’s total basket of trade is virtually unchanged. For India, this should reinforce the government’s resolve to pursue domestic reforms to improve competitiveness. There are no shortcuts to success.India’s more aggressive approach to signing trade agreements is often viewed as a “response” to uncertain U.S. trade policy under the Trump administration. While this may be an accelerant, India’s vigorous pursuit of deals started well before President Trump’s second term.India had a modestly aggressive trade policy from 2000 to 2011, largely focused on deals with Asian neighbors including Japan, Korea, ASEAN, Sri Lanka, and others. This “deal-friendly” period was politically agnostic, bridging the Vajpayee government into the Singh government. However, the deals themselves are more “political statements” than groundbreaking economic measures. The resulting agreements had significant exclusion lists. Tariff reductions were less expansive and spaced over longer periods of time.India then entered decade devoid of significant new agreements. India was a member of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Agreement (RCEP) talks but ultimately withdrew in 2019.Our program has noted many times before that the Modi government’s initial “Make in India” push was focused on protectionism. Starting in 2014, the government pursued a range of tariff and non-tariff barriers to provide a “safe space” for Indian manufacturing to bloom. The net result, per the World Bank, has been relative stagnation, with manufacturing hovering at 13% to 15% of GDP over the last decade. Fortunately, we have witnessed a refreshed approach to trade in recent years, focused on domestic support programs like the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) programs and the newly aggressive approach to trade deals.Two of the first agreements the Modi government concluded, with the United Arab Emirates and Australia, came into force in 2022 (the deal with Mauritius came into force slightly earlier, but trade is negligible, so it is not included it this assessment). Many others have followed including the Swiss-led EFTA block, Oman, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, and the European Union. These came into force in 2024-25, or will be in force in the year ahead.We now have several years of post-agreement data to examine how bilateral trade has evolved, although the figures alone cannot establish how much of that change was caused by the agreements. The headline numbers are quite good, as has been reported by multiple government and non-government bodies.Australia In the two fiscal years before the agreement came into force (FY20 and FY21), India-Australia total good trade averaged about $13b a year. In the most recent 2 fiscal years (FY25 & FY26), India-Australia total goods trade averaged about $23b a year. This marks a 76% increase in average annual trade. India’s average exports doubled from $4b annually to $8b annually during this period.United Arab Emirates (UAE) In the two fiscal years before the agreement came into force (FY20 and FY21), India-UAE total goods trade averaged $55b a year. In the most recent 2 fiscal years (FY25 & FY26), India-UAE total goods trade averaged $100b a year. This marks an 81% increase in average annual trade.India’s exports increased from $22b annually to $36b annually during this period.

Despite the growth in trade following these two agreements, neither country has substantially gained ground in terms of India’s total trade mix. Australia remains stuck at around 2 percent of India’s exports and imports, as part of the nation’s total basket of trade. India’s trade with the UAE as a percent of its total basket has grown modestly during this period, from around 7 percent of imports and exports to 8 percent of imports and exports.At the very least, there is no evidence supporting older Indian fears about trade agreements causing a flood of imports. However, there is also low evidence that trade agreements produce “quick wins” in terms of relative increases in trade, and particularly exports, with deal partners. Pushing ahead with difficult reforms in areas like land, labor, power, water, and judicial remediation will help India fulfill the promise of these new agreements.Note: All data drawn from the Indian Department of Commerce “Tradestat” portal, https://tradestat.commerce.gov.in/eidb/country_wise_ttrade
